assessment_summary:
Proof attempt:
1. Assume X_n converges to X in distribution. This means F_{X_n}(t) -> F_X(t) at all continuity points t of F_X.
2. We want to show that for any \epsilon > 0, P(|X_n - X| > \epsilon) -> 0 as n -> \infty.
3. The probability P(|X_n - X| > \epsilon) depends on the joint distribution of (X_n, X).
4. Since convergence in distribution only restricts the marginal distributions F_{X_n}, it does not provide enough information about the joint distribution to conclude that the distance |X_n - X| vanishes in probability.
The proof attempt fails at step 4 because we cannot guarantee that X_n and X are close to each other in the probability space just because their marginal cumulative distribution functions are close. A counterexample is needed.
counterexample: Let \Omega = {1, 2} with P({1}) = 0.5 and P({2}) = 0.5. Define X(1) = 1, X(2) = -1. Define X_n = -X for all n, so X_n(1) = -1, X_n(2) = 1. Both X and X_n take values 1 and -1 with probability 0.5 each. Thus, their cumulative distribution functions are identical for all n: F_{X_n}(t) = F_X(t) for all t. This implies F_{X_n}(t) -> F_X(t) for all continuity points t, meaning X_n converges to X in distribution. However, |X_n(\omega) - X(\omega)| = 2 for all \omega \in \Omega. For \epsilon = 1, P(|X_n - X| > 1) = P(2 > 1) = 1 for all n. The probability does not converge to 0, so X_n does not converge to X in probability.
